Review – Godzilla Minus Zero

  • Written by: Hugh Verheylewegen
  • November 6, 2026
  • Reviews, TV & Movies
  • godzilla
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 12:32
Instaread

Directed by Takashi Yamazaki, Godzilla Minus Zero is set two years after the events of Minus One, following the survivors who are struggling to rebuild after Godzilla’s destructive rampage nearly brought an end to Japan. But just as Japan attempts to recover from the devastation of the previous attack, a new catastrophe strikes in the form of a new monster, King Ghidorah, that threatens the entire world. This results in the survivors needing to take action once more just in time for the return of Godzilla, who regenerates and resurfaces to combat the new monster.

For 72 years Godzilla has ruled as one of cinema’s most iconic monsters and has continuously evolved through different forms of media, going through various tones that have allowed him to survive for so long. While the Monsterverse films have done a great job reviving investment into the character in recent years, it was Godzilla Minus One that truly recaptured the awe-inspiring terror Godzilla was known for in his 1954 debut, while also delivering an emotionally compelling human narrative that won the hearts of many around the world. Director Takashi Yamazaki and his team created a masterful entry into Godzilla’s long history, but now they were back with a sequel that was intended to be a bigger and bolder continuation of the story they had established, and needless to say I was very excited for it. On the night of Godzilla’s 72nd anniversary, I got to see the film on the biggest possible screen and it definitely was much bigger and bolder, delivering the most satisfying, epic, and emotionally impactful Godzilla sequel I have ever seen in my years as a lifelong fan.

Godzilla Minus Zero is a grand and worthy successor to Minus One, being a phenomenal blockbuster that doesn’t sacrifice its heart or impactful themes that made the first film so beloved but instead evolves them to new heights. It’s a film that perfectly balances a large-scale and brutal monster epic with a compelling human drama that explores many powerful and relevant themes such as the themes of fear, hatred, and trauma that war leaves behind. This film easily cements itself as not only one of the best films of this year but also as the best Godzilla sequel ever made in the 72-year-long existence of the character.

Before talking about the amazing human characters and the phenomenal cast members that play them, I do have to talk about the two iconic monsters, Godzilla and King Ghidorah, whose presence and destructive actions are more front and center in this film than expected and are brought to life through phenomenal VFX work. They don’t overstay their welcome, nor are they ever underused, but are treated as two terrifying titans of mass destruction that also symbolically represent various anti-war themes as well as themes of the struggles of post-war Japan.

Godzilla is back again bigger and better than ever! He takes a more chaotic neutral role in this film compared to his completely villainous role in Minus One, but is still treated as a terrifying and destructive monster whose attack on Japan two years ago has left lasting impacts on the human characters and the country itself. He still represents the physical embodiment of human-made nuclear horror that brings along terror and badass action but we also get to see how humans attempt to utilize him for their own purposes after his shocking return from death. Some seek to use him to help destroy the new monster, some seek to use him as a tool for revenge and some seek to study him for potential uses in warfare that could lead to the destruction of the entire world.

The evolution of Godzilla from being a symbol of survivor’s guilt for one man in the last film to being a relevant representation of ethical and moral use of power beyond comprehension in this film is beautifully written and makes Godzilla even more of terrifying figure outside of his destructive nature.

Serving as the primary villain of this sequel is King Ghidorah, the greatest archenemy of Godzilla’s history who we last saw clash with Godzilla on the big screen in 2019 with Godzilla: King of the Monsters. While the last modern adaptation of King Ghidorah wasn’t necessarily a bad one, it has nothing on the absolutely phenomenal adaptation this film provides for one of Godzilla’s greatest enemies. He is truly a terrifying alien monster that brings horrific death and destruction the very moment he is on screen and has been evolved to be deadlier than past iterations with new and updated powers. Besides a new look and new abilities, King Ghidorah is also given a new symbolic meaning outside of just being a monster for Godzilla to fight. While Godzilla represents human-made nuclear horror, Ghidorah’s manipulation of weather, lightning, and the skies acts as a metaphor for the devastating typhoons and natural calamities that battered postwar Japan, which further delayed the nation’s recovery at the time. Ghidorah is portrayed as an overwhelming, multi-front disaster that turns survival into an even more desperate battle for the characters and makes the narrative feel even more compelling. For me personally, this is the best portrayal of King Ghidorah we have ever received from Godzilla’s franchise history.

The human characters consist of returning faces along with new faces who are all given fantastic performances by their respective cast members making them all feel extremely compelling and impactful in their respective arcs. Each of the primary characters are grappling with lingering trauma and their duties to the future as they are once again called to action with the return of Godzilla and the rise of Ghidorah. Kōichi Shikishima, reprised by Ryunosuke Kamiki, has finally managed to move on from his guilt and chose to live for his now-wife Noriko and daughter Akiko. However, he has become increasingly protective of what he has now after almost losing it all that he will do anything to protect his family, even at the risk of endangering others’ lives by refusing the call to action. Circumstances end up changing this and you can’t help but feel very sympathetic for the struggles he and his family have to endure as a result of events caused by the monsters. The character’s suffering is all magnificently portrayed by Ryunosuke Kamiki, who continues to be the best leading performance in this film as he was in Minus One.

Also delivering a strong and heartfelt performance is Minami Hamabe as Noriko Shikishima, whose miraculous survival from Godzilla’s attack in Minus One has gifted her a second chance at life, but she has also been cursed by a parting gift of Godzilla. Like Kōichi, she is protective of her family and will do anything to protect them but when she learns of the consequences of her new condition and impending threat of both monsters, her life changes forever and she is forced to take drastic action. After everything she has been through alongside Kōichi, she deserves a peaceful life that she sadly can’t seem to have and it is heartbreaking to witness, especially with the beautiful performance she is given by Minami Hamabe.

Taking a more central role in this film is Kenji Noda, reprised by Hidetaka Yoshioka, who is now the director of the Large-Scale Disaster Response Bureau. Having been one of the heroes responsible for taking down Godzilla, he has now been burdened with the responsibility of helping Japan recover from its wounds and is faced with the overwhelming task of defeating two monsters that both threaten to destroy Japan and the world. Their vast destruction and god-like powers push Noda to make extremely hard and dangerous decisions that not only endanger his people but have the potential to change the world for the worse. He is given a tremendous performance by Hidetaka Yoshioka alongside Masami Nagasawa as Makoto Aoyama, a meteorologist and pupil to Noda who tries to help carry the burdens he wears on his shoulders.

The most unexpected phenomenal performance to come out of this film came from one of the newest characters named Professor Kanji Murakami, played by Min Tanaka, a biologist carrying deep psychological scars from the war as a survivor of the Hiroshima bombing. His character is a brilliant deep dive into the facets of trauma and the never-ending cycles of war/hatred between countries that gets explored in a very graphic fashion and plays hugely into the story when he discovers a shocking way to “manipulate” Godzilla for Japan’s needs. His inability to move on from his trauma and rage is immensely understanding but it is also shown to be incredibly dangerous given what his discovery can do to the world in the wrong hands.

This film’s narrative works both as an epic and high-stakes monster blockbuster and an emotionally impactful human drama that takes a lot of bold swings that end up hitting the mark beautifully due to masterful execution by Takashi Yamazaki and his team. The heartfelt family-centric elements, along with the post-war trauma elements from the first film, continue to play a huge part in this film’s story while also being greatly expanded upon with new additions that make this story feel bigger and better in all the right ways alongside its jaw-dropping action sequences. You care about everything in the story and not just the monsters only especially given how the monsters and their destructive action is intertwined with the anti-war themes this film provides just like with Minus One and the 1954 original film.

Many moral and ethical questions are presented throughout this film regarding meddling with powers beyond comprehension, the worth of standing up for what you believe, the dangers of vengeful pursuits, and living with wounds, fear, and trauma to the point it’s impossible to overcome them. These themes are presented through both the characters and the monsters, making them both equally compelling in the narrative and offering proper substance for the grand kaiju duel that this film builds up towards and pays off magnificently.

As much as I adore the epic and entertaining Kaiju fights that the Monsterverse has provided in their films, there is no denying that the grand Kaiju fight of this film felt way more powerful on an emotional scale given the stakes that are at play and the well-developed characters involved.

With this being the first Godzilla film to earn an R-rating, we see exactly why it was given it with this film delivering some of the most visceral and violent action ever depicted in a Godzilla film. From heads being ripped off to limbs being torn from their sockets and chunks of flesh being chewed out, this film doesn’t hold back from being all out bloody and making the Kaiju fight feel like a true fight to the death. So much graphic yet epic destruction and power is brought to life through fantastic VFX and cinematography that goes above and beyond everything we had seen in Minus One, which could likely be due to increased budget and the use of IMAX technology.

Enhancing things further for this film is ear-shattering yet phenomenal sound design and a haunting score, made by returning composer Naoki Satō, that really makes you fully immersed in the feels of danger, desolation and powerlessness facing mass destruction that is depicted on the big screen. The classic Godzilla theme gets an expected upgrade in this film, but I was shocked to find how spine-chilling and hair standing the new theme for King Ghidorah was, with the way it builds up tension and dread for Godzilla’s greatest foe.

Minus Zero was everything I wanted for a sequel to Minus One while also being so much more with its evolution of the characters, themes and thrilling monster action that doesn’t sacrifice the heart that made it’s predecessor so special. This is a bigger, better and bolder film that I absolutely loved from start to end and cements itself as another one of my favorite Godzilla films of all time next to the first one. It’s a truly phenomenal experience that needs to be seen on the biggest screen rather than at home especially if you were someone who loved the first film. This is one Godzilla sequel you don’t want to miss! I’m going to give Godzilla Minus Zero an A+ = 100.
